parts.partTitle: Why CPUs Break Your Java Code

beats.headline: Why does your code work on your laptop but crash in production?
beats.subline: It is not your logic, it is the CPU architecture.
beats.narration: Your code runs perfectly on your Intel laptop but fails on AWS Graviton. Why? Because CPUs don't read from RAM directly. They use registers, store buffers, and L1 caches that lead to hidden memory reordering.

beats.title: The Hardware Reality
beats.subtitle: Cores don't talk to RAM directly
beats.narration: Each CPU core has private caches and store buffers. A write in Core 1 might sit in a buffer, invisible to Core 2. The JMM is the contract that forces these cores to sync up.

beats.title: x86 vs. ARM64
beats.narration: x86 chips are naturally stricter. ARM chips are aggressive, reordering loads and stores for speed. If you don't follow JMM rules, your code will break on modern cloud infrastructure.

beats.title: The Reordering Hazard

steps.explanation: Result r1=0, r2=0 is actually legal!

beats.narration: In this classic example, both threads could finish with r1 and r2 equal to zero. Because the operations are independent, the CPU reorders them, violating your intuitive expectations.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In

beats.narration: That is the hardware trap. In Part 2, we see how JIT hoisting turns your loop into an infinite hang.

beats.headline: Why does your worker thread never stop?
beats.subline: The JIT compiler is smarter than your loop.
beats.narration: You have a boolean flag to stop a thread. You set it to true, but the worker keeps running. It is not a bug in your logic; it is the JIT compiler optimizing your code into oblivion.

beats.title: The Invisible Flag
beats.narration: Because stopRequested isn't volatile, the JIT compiler sees that nothing inside the loop changes it. It hoists the read outside the loop, effectively turning your code into a while true loop.

beats.title: The Debugger Deception

lines.text: # Adding a print statement fixes it?

beats.narration: Ever notice the bug vanishes when you add a print statement? That is because PrintStream is synchronized. It forces a memory barrier, flushing caches and preventing the JIT from hoisting the loop.

beats.title: Before vs. After Volatile
beats.narration: Adding volatile tells the JVM: don't cache this in a register, and don't assume it's constant. It forces a read from memory every single time.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): The volatile keyword deep dive →
beats.narration: Volatile is the fix. In Part 3, we break down exactly how it works under the hood.

beats.headline: Is volatile just a memory flag?
beats.subline: It is a hardware fence that stops CPU reordering.
beats.narration: Volatile is more than just visibility. It is a hardware barrier. It tells the CPU to flush its store buffers and stop reordering instructions around the access.

beats.title: Volatile Write Barrier
beats.subtitle: How the CPU enforces order
beats.narration: When you write to a volatile field, the JVM inserts a StoreStore barrier before and a StoreLoad barrier after. This ensures all previous writes are visible before the volatile write happens.

beats.title: The Atomic Counter Myth
beats.narration: Common mistake: thinking volatile makes count++ atomic. It doesn't. It is three separate bytecode operations. Two threads can read 5, compute 6, and write 6, losing an update.

beats.title: Volatile vs. Atomic
beats.narration: Use volatile for flags or replacing immutable references. Use AtomicInteger or LongAdder for counters. Don't mix them up.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.narration: Volatile is powerful, but limited. In Part 4, we unlock the Happens-Before rules to master synchronization.

beats.headline: What does 'happens-before' actually mean?
beats.subline: It is not about time; it is about visibility.
beats.narration: Happens-before isn't about wall-clock time. It is a formal guarantee that memory writes in one thread are visible to another. If you don't have a happens-before edge, you have a race condition.

beats.title: The Happens-Before Chain
beats.subtitle: Transitivity is your best friend
beats.narration: If Thread 1 writes data and then a volatile flag, and Thread 2 reads that flag, Thread 2 is guaranteed to see the data. This is the magic of transitivity.

beats.title: Safe Piggybacking

steps.explanation: Visible to any thread reading ready.

beats.narration: You don't need to make the data volatile. Because ready is volatile, the write to data is guaranteed to be visible to any thread that reads ready as true. This is safe piggybacking.

beats.title: Rules of Engagement
beats.narration: Every synchronized block and every join call creates a happens-before edge. These are the building blocks of thread-safe Java applications.

beats.title: Part 4 Locked In
beats.narration: You now know the rules. In Part 5, we fix the classic Double-Checked Locking bug.

beats.headline: Why is your singleton broken?
beats.subline: Double-checked locking without volatile is a disaster.
beats.narration: Double-checked locking is a classic interview question. If you don't use volatile, you aren't just risking performance; you're risking returning a partially initialized object.

beats.title: The Broken Singleton
beats.narration: The JVM can assign the reference before the constructor finishes. Another thread sees a non-null instance and returns it, but the fields are still null. Total chaos.

beats.title: The Fix
beats.narration: Just add volatile. That single keyword creates the happens-before edge that ensures the constructor finishes before the reference is published.

beats.title: The Modern Way

lines.text: private static class Holder { static final Singleton INSTANCE = new Singleton(); }

beats.narration: Better yet, use the Holder idiom. The classloader handles the synchronization for you. It is cleaner, faster, and impossible to get wrong.
